title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI system deployed in an automated software release workflow accepted unvalidated input from any GitHub user and processed it through an LLM without human review. The system had broad permissions to publish code to multiple package repositories. A prompt injection vulnerability allowed an attacker to manipulate the AI's behavior to execute arbitrary code and steal publishing credentials, potentially enabling supply chain attacks against millions of developers.

The failure occurred in the deployment model itself: a high-risk operation was fully automated with AI decision-making and no human gate. Catching this would have required either restricting who could trigger the workflow, validating inputs before passing them to the LLM, requiring human approval before publishing releases, or rotating credentials regularly enough to limit exposure. None of these controls were in place.

It is not established that any malicious package was actually published, only that the vulnerability existed and evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit it.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability between late December 2025 and February 2026. The vulnerability existed in an automated issue triage workflow powered by Claude AI that ran with broad permissions and accepted input from anyone with a GitHub account. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that attackers could exploit a prompt injection flaw in the workflow to execute arbitrary code, then use a cache poisoning technique to steal publishing credentials for the Visual Studio Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM package repositories.

The attack chain would have allowed malicious actors to publish compromised versions of Cline to millions of developers worldwide. Khan repeatedly attempted to contact Cline's team starting January 1st through multiple channels without receiving a response. After public disclosure on February 9th, 2026, Cline fixed the vulnerability within an hour by removing the AI workflow and updating their publishing processes. Cline later confirmed they rotated all relevant credentials and found evidence suggesting someone may have attempted exploitation, though no malicious updates were confirmed to have been released.
